items.summary: arXiv:2610.28886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-b…
items.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges

items.summary: The Adaptive Agentic Intelligence Framework (AAIF), built with Strands Agents, handles routine tasks locally with small language models and routes complex requests to cloud models through Amazon Bedrock. This post walks through building AAIF with local SLMs through Ollama and Amazon Bedrock, using an Internet of Things monitoring scenario.
items.title: Adaptive agentic intelligence framework using Strands Agents

items.summary: arXiv:2610.27032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by direc…
items.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement

items.summary: arXiv:2610.27279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. items.title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion

items.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use

items.summary: arXiv:2610.27518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every day, more than 40 million people ask ChatGPT a health question, such as whether laptop posture explains a stiff neck and days of pounding headache. Posture is plausible, but meningitis is a time-critical possibility. We introduce SelfDx, a paired benchmark for whether models have the appropriate response behavior, a form of epistemic independence, in health questions where misplaced agreement with the user's self-diagnosis could delay urgent or emergency care. items.title: When Health Assistants Agree Too Readily: A Benchmark of Time-Critical Self-Diagnosis

items.summary: arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. items.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets

items.summary: arXiv:2610.28819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the ability of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be verified programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints, pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-access, and cannot be easily extended. We present Lift-Bench, an IF benchmark that asks a model to draft a docum…
items.title: LIFT: Scoped Constraints for Evaluating and Training Instruction Following

items.summary: arXiv:2610.29052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whos…
items.title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models

items.summary: arXiv:2610.28977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. items.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study

items.summary: arXiv:2610.28937v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. items.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift

items.summary: Teams deploying custom text-to-speech models on Amazon SageMaker AI often guess at autoscaling thresholds, and a wrong guess either wastes GPU spend or breaches a latency SLO. This post deploys Kokoro-82M as a custom container and derives a measured autoscaling policy from two live-endpoint measurements, Q_max and T_total, instead of guesswork.
items.title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI

items.summary: Many teams build a multi-agent AI prototype in days but hit a wall in production. This post defines five production challenges (orchestration, per-agent model selection, reliable operation, secure code execution, and monitoring) and shows how Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent system on AWS, solves each.
items.title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them
